items.answer_reason: Two of six equally likely faces, 5 and 6, are greater than 4; 2/6 = 1/3.
issues: The wrong fractions are distinct but are mainly generic numerical guesses; 2/3 can be read as counting the four nonmatching faces.

items.answer_reason: After the first red marble is removed, 4 red and 3 blue marbles remain, so the chance is 4/7.
issues: Distractors reflect several possible failures to update the numerator or denominator, but 4/8 is equivalent to 1/2 and still unambiguously wrong.
1/3 is a weak distractor without an evident misconception in this two-flip setup; 1/2 and 3/4 are more interpretable errors.

items.answer_reason: The four equal outcomes have mean ($1 + $2 + $3 + $4)/4 = $2.50.
issues: $1.00 is a weak distractor for an expected value over four equally likely positive amounts; the other wrong amounts are likewise simple numeric guesses.

items.answer_reason: P(A)P(B) = 0.5 times 0.4 = 0.2, equal to the stated P(A and B), so the events meet the definition of independence.
issues: The correct option is the only one using the defining product-versus-intersection comparison; this is legitimate mathematical content, although the distractors are fairly easy to eliminate if the definition is known.

items.answer_reason: Passing and failing are complementary outcomes for the stated test, so P(fail) = 1 - 0.85 = 0.15.
issues: The wording assumes a component either passes or fails; this is normal for an introductory probability item but could be stated explicitly. 0.75 and 0.50 are weak distractors without a clear calculation path.

items.answer_reason: Mutually exclusive events have no overlap, so P(A or B) = 0.3 + 0.45 = 0.75.
issues: 1.00 is a weak distractor because the given probabilities sum below one; 0.135 does represent the mistaken multiplication operation.
